title: Typed Extension Discovery and Backward Shimming Playbook
author: Riley Chen
content:
Overview:
This playbook defines a pragmatic, engineering-friendly approach for discovering typed API extensions and serving backward-compatible responses via shims. It focuses on model-serving and edge APIs where schema changes, optional extensions, and hosted client diversity create compatibility risk. The guidance balances strict typing for server-side validation with flexible runtime shimming to preserve client behavior and avoid mass client updates.

Goals:
- Provide a predictable discovery protocol so clients and services can negotiate optional extensions without full deployment coordination.
- Define a small set of supported extension patterns and canonical shims that maintain observable semantics for downstream consumers.
- Establish rollout, testing, telemetry, and alerting practices to detect compatibility regressions early.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood public inference APIs, internal service-to-service RPCs that return structured outputs (JSON or protobuf), and streaming session responses.
- Not intended for: complete breaking schema redesigns, contract-first public SDKs without a migration window, or binary wire-format incompatibilities.

Key Definitions:
- Base Contract: the canonical response schema version that clients are guaranteed to understand (e.g., v1.2.0).
- Extension Field: a non-required field added to the schema with clearly documented type and semantics.
- Discovery Header/Frame: a metadata mechanism (HTTP header or initial streaming frame) that advertises supported extensions and server capabilities.
- Shim: server-side transformation that produces a response compatible with older clients by removing/transforming new fields or mapping new enums to legacy values.

Discovery and Negotiation:
1) Discovery header (HTTP): services must advertise supported schema features in a single header named X-RW-API-Features. Format: comma-separated tokens with optional versioned suffixes. Example: X-RW-API-Features: structured-embeddings:v2,role-metadata:v1.
2) Streaming: the initial control frame must include a features list and a shard of the chosen model variant. Example JSON control frame: {"features": ["role-metadata:v1"], "variant": "redwood-base-1"}.
3) Client hints: clients may include Accept-Extensions header to request opt-in fields. Servers must respect client hints for opt-in extensions but may still send non-critical fields when safe.

Extension Pattern Catalog (supported):
- Optional scalar fields: must be nullable or absent when unknown.
- Namespaced extension objects: fields grouped under an extensions map (recommended key: "x_rw_extensions"). Example: "x_rw_extensions": { "safety_flags": {...} }
- Enum additive expansion: new enum values must include a legacy fallback mapping in the contract manifest.
- Versioned sub-schemas: complex extensions with their own schema version (e.g., "summarization:v2").

Shim Strategies (server-side):
1) Remove-for-legacy: strip unknown optional fields before sending to clients that don’t advertise the extension. Use when the field is purely additive and no behavior changes are required.
2) Fallback-mapping: convert new enum values or structured objects into legacy representations using declared mapping rules. Maintain mapping table in service config.
3) Simulated-synthesis: if an extension provides higher-fidelity output, produce a synthesized legacy surrogate when possible (e.g., reduce structured answer to plain text summary). Only use when synthesis is deterministic and well-tested.
4) Dual-response (conditional): for a small set of high-value clients, send both new-typed payload and a legacy wrapper under a single response envelope where bandwidth and client parsing permit.

Compatibility Manifest (service config) — required fields and example:
- service: inference-gateway
- base_contract: v1.3.0
- supported_extensions: ["role-metadata:v1", "structured-embeddings:v2"]
- default_shim_policy: remove-for-legacy
- enum_mappings: [{"field": "sentiment", "mapping": {"very_positive": "positive", "very_negative": "negative"}}]

Testing and Validation:
- Unit tests: every new extension must ship with unit tests for shim logic and mapping tables.
- Contract tests: add a contract suite run in CI that exercises:
  1) feature discovery header permutations
  2) Accept-Extensions variations
  3) shim policy correctness (strip/map/synthesize)
- Synthetic production canary: deploy a canary that mirrors traffic to a shadow instance where new extensions are enabled and verify parity metrics (error rate, token delta, latency) over 24–72 hours.

Observable Signals and Alerts:
Essential metrics (per-route, per-model):
- shim_rate: percentage of responses altered by a shim (SLO target: < 2% for stable releases).
- extension_usage: count of requests that accepted or requested each extension.
- mapping_failures: count of enum mapping anomalies (alert if > 0.1% over 1h).
- client_parse_errors: 4xx/5xx originating from downstream client integrations (alert threshold depends on client tier).
- response_size_delta: average bytes added/removed by shims (monitor for unexpected growth).

Alerting rules (examples):
- P1: mapping_failures rate > 0.1% sustained for 15m -> Pager (team: runtime).
- P2: shim_rate > 10% with extension_usage < 1% -> Slack alert to owners (indicates misconfiguration).
- P3: client_parse_errors spike correlated with a recent extension rollout -> Notify owners and pause rollout.

Rollout and Canary Guidance:
1) Feature flag gating: every extension must be behind a rollout flag. Feature flag should control: discovery header advertisement, field emission, and shim policy.
2) Phased rollout:
  a) Internal-only (10% traffic; engineering org)
  b) Beta customers (+ selected enterprise customers)
  c) Gradual ramp to 100% with automated health checks at 5/25/50/100%
3) Rollback criteria: any of the following observed within the rollout window -> automatic rollback: mapping_failures > threshold, client_parse_errors up > 30%, error rate increase > 0.5%.

Operational Runbook (quick):
1) If an alert fires for mapping_failures:
  a) Identify the mapping table and recent commits via service config history.
  b) Run the contract test locally against the canary binary.
  c) If mapping is incorrect, update mapping in config and deploy hotfix to canary; if unsure, pause advertisement by toggling discovery header.
2) If client_parse_errors spike:
  a) Correlate client user agents and ingress tokens.
  b) Revert extension advertisement for affected routes and roll back at traffic layer.
  c) Engage customer success for impacted customers.

Ownership and Governance:
- Service owner: runtime-api-team (primary), with policy stewardship by API standards working group.
- Extensions registry steward: model-onboarding (maintains canonical list of extension tokens and schema links).
- Quarterly review: Every extension must be reviewed by API standards working group for lifecycle (deprecation, promotion to base contract).

Migration Checklist for Promoting an Extension to Base Contract:
1) At least 90 days of stable usage and < 0.05% mapping_failures.
2) Client adoption > 80% for internally vetted clients or a signed delivery plan for external SDKs.
3) All shims and mappings audited and checked into the config repo.
4) Update public API docs, SDK changelogs, and release notes.

Example snippets:
- Discovery header example:
  curl -v -H "X-RW-API-Features: role-metadata:v1,structured-embeddings:v2" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate"

- Shim mapping example (YAML):
  enum_mappings:
    sentiment:
      very_positive: positive
      very_negative: negative

Checklist for engineers adding an extension:
- [ ] Add extension token and schema doc to extensions registry (model-onboarding).
- [ ] Draft mapping rules and shim policy in service config.
- [ ] Add unit and contract tests.
- [ ] Instrument shim_rate, mapping_failures, extension_usage.
- [ ] Run synthetic canary for 72 hours.
- [ ] Schedule API standards review within 2 weeks of initial canary.
